items.label: A
items.critique: Flat, transactional shop-and-trainer lines with a price and a yes/no question, the slangy 'Ya want one?' and the dry field-guide-to-spiders explanation are pure Nox.

items.label: B
items.critique: Lively, but the run-on second page with nested clauses, the 'Take these potions -- and some gold' reward-at-the-ask pattern and the doubled 'Bless you' outcomes read like a careful pastiche rather than Westwood's terser lines.

items.label: C
items.critique: Short, slightly odd and unpolished ('hit that red button on the wall', 'Basic training isn't for everyone') with a gag outcome; exactly Westwood's offhand register.

items.label: D
items.critique: Every beat is spelled out (direction, item that helps, reward, follow-up contact) and the '?!' and stacked exclamations feel manufactured; 'Smuggling's hard enough with the Trolls about!' is a written-for-flavour line.

items.label: E
items.critique: Two interlocking quests with cross-referenced townsfolk, a guessing-game opener and polished comic voice; Westwood's quest-givers rarely layer exposition and characterization this densely.

items.label: F
items.critique: The used-car-salesman joke ('only used it on weekends'), 'There ya go!' and the pushy refusal line are Westwood's anachronistic humour in short sentences.

items.label: G
items.critique: An absurd 50,000-gold offer, 'lad', mild run-on farewells and plain logistics; slightly clumsy in the way the original is.

items.label: H
items.critique: Panicked openers, 'What kept you!?', a dangling '... Hello? Is anybody still out there?' gag and rewards plus future favours in every outcome feel engineered; too many exclamations per page.

tells: New texts hand over items at the ask ('Take these potions/boots/whistle') and stack rewards plus a future favour in the outcome; Westwood's quest lines usually state one price or one task and one plain result.
New texts run to three or four pages per ask with every quest beat spelled out (who did it, where to go, which tool helps); Westwood's are often one or two short sentences.
Interrobangs ('?!', '!?') and long chains of exclamations mark the new texts; Westwood punctuates more flatly.
Westwood's humour is anachronistic and deadpan (weekend bow, field guide to spiders, absurd prices); the new humour is situational slapstick and character banter built for the scene.
New texts cross-reference other named townsfolk and plant follow-up hooks ('He'll meet you at the top', 'a rider came asking for you'); Westwood's lines rarely tie quests together in dialogue.
Westwood's lines are often transactional (gold amount, 'Do you accept?', 'You want it?') and slightly unpolished; the new texts are uniformly polished and vivid.
